changes.before: Replace the element assignment with scores = new int[]{9}. What happens?
changes.after: Separate a shared class field from a variable that cannot be reassigned.

before: A static field belongs to the class rather than each instance. Ticket.issued counts constructor calls in this single-threaded example. Each Ticket still has its own final number assigned once by its constructor.

A final variable cannot be reassigned after initialization. If it holds an object or array reference, the referenced contents may still be mutable. final int[] scores fixes the array reference, not every array element.
static controls whether a field is class-wide; final controls assignment to the variable. Neither alone is a synchronization policy for concurrent mutation.

Expected output or behavior: 1 2 2
9
. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Contrast a final StringBuilder reference with its mutable text content. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A static field belongs to the class, so the Ticket objects here share issued. Each constructor call increases that shared count. This example makes the tickets one at a time.
A final variable can be assigned only once. Each Ticket has its own final number, set by its constructor. Later code cannot assign a different number to that field.
For an array reference, final fixes which array the variable points to. It does not freeze the array's items. Changing scores[0] is allowed; assigning a different array to scores is not.
The first line prints 1 2 2: the two ticket numbers and the shared count. The next line prints 9 because the array item changed while its reference stayed the same.
The quiz replaces the whole scores reference instead of changing one item. Apply final's rule to the variable being assigned.

before.question: Replace the element assignment with scores = new int[]{9}. What happens?
choices: The original array is silently copied
It compiles because arrays are mutable
Compilation rejects reassigning the final reference
before.explanation: Mutating an element was permitted, but replacing the reference stored in final scores is a different, forbidden assignment.

after.question: Replace scores[0] = 9; with scores = new int[]{9};. What happens?
choices: Java silently copies the original array.
It compiles because array items can change.
Compilation fails because scores is a final reference.
after.explanation: The original line changes an item. The new line tries to assign a second reference to the final variable scores, which is not allowed.
